records.table: Colonel E. H. Taylor is the Buffalo Trace bourbon named for the Frankfort distiller who fought for the Bottled-in-Bond Act of 1897. The Small Batch Bottled in Bond is his law in a bottle, one season at 100 proof: caramel corn, butterscotch and pepper.
records.story: Edmund Haynes Taylor Jr. (1830 to 1923) was a Frankfort banker, sixteen years the town's mayor, and a distiller who wanted a buyer to be able to trust a bottle of bourbon. Around 1870 he bought a small distillery at Leestown, beside Frankfort, and christened it O.F.C. When he fell into debt, George T. Stagg took the distillery over in 1878 and kept Taylor on to run it, and by Buffalo Trace's account Taylor built its Warehouse C in 1885; the site became Buffalo Trace. In 1887 Taylor built a new distillery on Glenn's Creek in Woodford County, the castle that made Old Taylor. He pressed Congress for a law that would let a distiller age whiskey in a government bonded warehouse and sell it under a federal stamp that vouched for its season, its age and its strength, and the Bottled-in-Bond Act passed in 1897. In 2009 Buffalo Trace bought the Old Taylor label and its barrels from Beam, and it later began a line of bourbons in the colonel's full name. Of that line, the Small Batch is the bottle a bar keeps open, and it puts the bond before a guest on one label: the law, and the name of the man who fought for it.

records.table: New Riff is the distillery at Newport, Kentucky, across the Ohio River from Cincinnati, that sold no bourbon of its own make until it could be bonded. Its Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey Bottled in Bond is 30 per cent rye at 100 proof: butterscotch and oak, then clove.
records.story: New Riff opened its doors in May 2014 at Newport, on the Kentucky bank of the Ohio River facing Cincinnati. Its founders, who came from a Northern Kentucky drinks shop, set out to make bourbon of the distillery's own make, and resolved that none would go on sale until it met the rule of 1897: one season, one distillery, at least four years in a bonded warehouse and exactly 100 proof. The distillery settled on a mash of 65 per cent corn, 30 rye and 5 malted barley, soured and fermented in open tanks and distilled on the grain through a tall copper column still and a doubler, the method it calls the Kentucky Regimen. Four years on, in August 2018, the first bourbon distilled at Newport went on sale at the distillery, bottled in bond and without chill filtration, and it reached other states that autumn. Single barrel bottlings of the same mash followed, and in 2024 an eight year old. The bonded bourbon answers a guest who takes the bond for the old houses' word alone: a young distillery took it up as its promise of where and when its whiskey was made, and kept it on its standard bottle.

records.story: From Wales, Evan Williams (1755 to 1810) came to Kentucky and settled at Louisville, and the label carries his name. A state historical marker there says he built a distillery on the Ohio River in 1783 and that it is said to have been the first commercial distillery in Kentucky; historians have questioned both the date and the claim, so they are told as tradition. The bourbon came much later. Heaven Hill was founded at Bardstown in 1935 by five brothers of a local family and a group of investors, and it introduced Evan Williams in 1957. When fire took the Bardstown distillery and seven of its warehouses on 7 November 1996, Heaven Hill turned to Louisville: it bought the Bernheim Distillery there in 1999, and from then on Bernheim distilled the bourbon for ageing and bottling at Bardstown. Beside the black label at 86 proof stands the white label, the brand's bottle of the bond. Every pour of it carries the whole bond: the house recipe, held to one season, four years and 100 proof.

records.story: Heaven Hill filled its first barrel at Bardstown on 13 December 1935, as the Old Heavenhill Springs distillery, founded by five brothers of a Bardstown family and a group of local investors; the brothers soon bought their partners out. The name, the company says, is that of the farmer who had owned the land, split in two by a clerk's slip on the paperwork sent to Frankfort and never mended. The house grew into a maker of many labels, among them Evan Williams from 1957. On 7 November 1996 fire swept seven of its warehouses and destroyed the Bardstown distillery, and in 1999 Heaven Hill bought the Bernheim Distillery in Louisville and moved its distilling there. For years a six year old bonded bourbon under the house's own name was sold only in Kentucky; it was retired in 2018, and in June 2019 Heaven Hill announced the 7 Year Old in its place, the same recipe with a year more in oak. In 2025 the house filled the first barrel at a new distillery in Bardstown, Heaven Hill Springs. Two promises stack on the 7 Year Old's label, and a guest can be shown both: the bond, and an age stated in words on the front.

records.story: Henry McKenna (1819 to 1893) left County Derry in Ireland for Kentucky and settled at Fairfield, a small town north east of Bardstown in Nelson County. There he went into business, and his whiskey, sold under his own name, came from a farm distillery that the label dates to 1855, the year its face prints. After his death in 1893 his sons carried the distillery on, and in 1941 the family sold it and the brand to Joseph E. Seagram and Sons. The domestic rights to the name later passed to Heaven Hill, a few miles away in Bardstown. In 1994, by Heaven Hill's account, the house added a single barrel bottling of the label, ten years old and bottled in bond, each bottle marked by hand with its barrel number and the day the barrel was filled. From 1999 Heaven Hill distilled it at its Bernheim Distillery in Louisville. An age statement, a single barrel and the bond can all be taught from it, and the handwritten barrel number makes the second plain to a guest.

quiz.q: A guest asks what the handwritten line on the front of a Henry McKenna single barrel bottle records. What is it?
quiz.explain: Each label carries the barrel's number and the day it was filled, in handwriting; the bottling day is not on that line, which dates the barrel, not the bottle.

quiz.q: Henry McKenna, the Irishman behind the label, settled and distilled in which Kentucky town?
quiz.explain: He settled at Fairfield in Nelson County; Bardstown is the nearby town where Heaven Hill ages the bourbon.

report: The plan's note is settled: Henry McKenna is dated 1819 to 1893. The birth year (9 January 1819, County Derry) stands in Whiskey University and the Kentucky Distillers' Association story; the death in 1893, when his sons took over, in a brand history and Whiskey University, and one account gives his age at death as 75.

The year 1855 is the label's own Est. 1855, in Heaven Hill's packaging release, and it is the year several accounts give for the distillery; the Kentucky Historical Society, as summarised, puts his move to Fairfield in 1851 and one source makes 1855 the year he opened a flour mill, so the story hedges it as the label's date.

The 1994 launch of the single barrel rests on Heaven Hill's own release as the Kentucky Distillers' Association reprinted it. The house's claim that it is the only ten year bonded single barrel bourbon is left out, as the voice refuses an only.

The year Heaven Hill took over the domestic rights from Seagram was not found (one account says the early 1980s), so the story gives no year and uses no word of sale for that step. The 1941 sale to Seagram stands in VinePair and a brand history; sources differ on whether a son died in 1940 or 1941, and the record leaves the sons unnamed.
The mash bill is Heaven Hill's blog's, which gives the same recipe for the namesake bonded bourbon and Henry McKenna; another Heaven Hill post speaks only of its bourbon rye mash bill.

Left out for want of a second source: the Irish distiller McKenna hired, the medicinal whiskey the family is said to have sold, and any figure for the barrels chosen each year. Sour Mash at 80 proof in others rests on Heaven Hill's packaging release and the Kentucky Distillers' Association report of it.

changed: story: the bourbon is now told as distilled at Bernheim from 1999, not since, for the same reason as in the Heaven Hill record.
